limits: Chapter treats only linear (or basis-expanded) boundaries; non-separable hyperplane case deferred to Chapter 12 (SVM).
Vowel and heart-disease results are single-dataset illustrations; train/test sizes for the vowel data are not given in this chapter; no variance or repeated-split numbers.
Authors concede the vowel train/test gap is partly due to repeated measurements on few individuals, different in train and test.
Efron 30% efficiency loss holds only if class densities are truly Gaussian; the authors note LDA is not robust to gross outliers.
Logistic regression convergence is not guaranteed (step-size halving suggested); glmnet/glmpath-era software (2007-2010) is dated.
practices: Treat LDA and QDA as always-available baselines; they win often because simple boundaries have low variance (p.111).
With K>=3 classes avoid regression on the indicator matrix because of masking; use LDA or logistic regression (p.105-106).
Choose RDA's alpha (and gamma) by validation data or cross-validation (p.112).
For two classes, derive the LDA direction by any method and then pick the cut-point that minimizes training error (p.116).
Fit logistic regression by maximum likelihood with Newton-Raphson/IRLS starting at beta=0, with step halving if the log-likelihood falls (p.120).
Interpret Wald Z scores with caution under correlated predictors; do model selection by backward elimination or analysis of deviance (p.122-123).
For L1-regularized logistic regression standardize predictors and do not penalize the intercept (p.125).
Prefer logistic regression as the safer bet (fewer assumptions), noting results are usually very similar to LDA (p.128).
Use an enlarged basis h(X) to get quadratic or richer boundaries from linear methods (p.102).
